text:
In the late summer of 1854, a ferocious outbreak of cholera struck the crowded Soho district of London, and within about ten days more than five hundred people living within a few hundred yards of one another had died. Cholera is a disease that causes violent diarrhea and vomiting, so severe that victims can lose their body's water within hours and die of it, and in the nineteenth century nobody knew what caused it. The prevailing view held that diseases like this spread through "miasma," a poisonous vapor rising from rotting matter and foul air, and the reasoning seemed sensible in a city where the smell of sewage and refuse was everywhere. John Snow, a physician who had pioneered the use of anesthesia and had attended Queen Victoria during childbirth, had long doubted this. He had come to suspect that cholera was carried in something people swallowed, most likely contaminated water, because the illness struck the gut first and seemed to follow the movements of people rather than the drift of air.

Snow lived near Broad Street and knew the area, and when the outbreak began he set out to test his idea against the evidence on the ground. He went door to door, asked families where they had gotten their drinking water, and obtained from the registrar's office the names and addresses of the dead. He then marked each death on a map of the neighborhood, with a small bar for every fatality stacked at the address where it occurred. The deaths clustered heavily around a public water pump on Broad Street, one of many pumps from which residents drew their water in an age before piped supplies reached individual homes, and the pattern was hard to read as anything but a pointer to that pump. Snow understood, however, that a pattern on a map could be explained away, so he looked for the people who did not fit it and found that these exceptions were more persuasive than the cases that did.

A workhouse near the pump, housing some five hundred people, had suffered only a handful of deaths, and Snow learned that it had its own well and so did not rely on the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street reported no cases among its workers, who by custom drank the beer provided to them and, it seems, the water from a well on the premises. Then there was a woman living far from Soho, in Hampstead, who died of cholera after her sons had carried bottles of Broad Street water to her, because she had once lived in the neighborhood and preferred its taste. A second woman who died in the same period was connected to the pump in the same way. These cases showed that people who drank the water fell ill wherever they lived, and people who lived beside the pump but did not drink its water mostly did not.

On the evening of 7 September, Snow took his findings to the board of guardians of St James's parish, the local authority responsible for the district, and urged them to act. The board was skeptical of his theory, but it agreed, perhaps because the evidence was so concrete and the remedy so cheap, to remove the handle from the pump, which made it impossible to draw water. The outbreak was already waning by then, since many residents had fled the area and many of the most susceptible had already died, and so the removal of the handle cannot be credited with ending the epidemic, a point that Snow himself acknowledged. What he cared about was the cause, and for this he pressed further, looking into the history of the pump and the house next to it.

The clergyman Henry Whitehead, who had at first doubted Snow's theory and set out to disprove it, ended up as his most valuable ally. Whitehead knew the neighborhood's residents personally and could trace which families had been affected and how, and he discovered that the first case of the outbreak was an infant girl who lived at 40 Broad Street, whose illness began just before the epidemic took off. Her mother had washed the baby's soiled diapers and thrown the water into a cesspool beneath the house, and an inspection later showed that the cesspool was close enough to the well that sewage could seep through the brickwork into the water below. The source of the contamination had been found, and with it a plausible chain from one sick infant to hundreds of deaths.

Snow's work did not win immediate acceptance, and the official inquiries of the time concluded that there was insufficient evidence to blame the water, in part because the scientific tools to see the cause directly did not yet exist. The bacterium responsible, Vibrio cholerae, had in fact been observed by the Italian scientist Filippo Pacini in the same year, but his work went almost unnoticed, and Robert Koch's later identification of the organism in the 1880s was what finally vindicated the water-borne theory. Snow died in 1858, never knowing that he had been proved right. His map and his method, which combined the plotting of cases in space, the search for exceptions, and the patient tracing of a disease to its source, are now regarded as founding moments of modern epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread through populations and how that spread can be stopped.
